title: Abu Bakr leads the prayer
hookLine: too weak to lead, he asks Abu Bakr to lead the prayer

lines: HE TRIES TO RISE, AND FAINTS.
cards: A parent hands over the car keys for the last time. A coach sits on the bench while someone else runs practice. Handing over the thing you always did is its own kind of hard.
For years in Medina, day after day, the Prophet ﷺ had usually stood at the front of the mosque and led the prayer. Now the call went up. He tried to get up to go, and fainted.
He came to, asked if the people had prayed, tried again, and fainted again. Next door, the people waited in the mosque.

teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari records what he said: tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer.

Aisha, Abu Bakr's own daughter, pushed back. Her father was a tender-hearted man, she said; whenever he recited the Qur'an he wept, and in the Prophet's place the people wouldn't hear him for his crying.
The Prophet repeated it: tell Abu Bakr to lead. So for those last days, Abu Bakr stood at the front, and the Prophet lay in the room next door.
The one who leads the prayer is the imam, from a root meaning to be in front. Then comes a moment the reports treasure. One day he felt a little better and came out, leaning on two men.
Abu Bakr heard him and began to step back to make room.
The Prophet signaled: stay where you are. He sat down beside Abu Bakr and prayed.
Aisha's report adds that Abu Bakr then followed the Prophet's prayer, standing, and the people followed Abu Bakr's, so the man at the front carried the movements of the man sitting beside him.
Jurists have long discussed what that means for who was leading. What the report shows is that he did not send his friend back into the rows. Muslims later read this scene in different ways.
Sunni scholars have often read it as a sign pointing toward Abu Bakr leading the community after him. Shia Muslims read the succession differently and hold that the Prophet named 'Ali.
Through those last days, the story shows a man who let another lead.

how: In congregational prayer Muslims follow one imam, who stands in front and whose movements everyone follows; the story of Abu Bakr leading in the Prophet's last days is often told when explaining who should lead the prayer.

o: a teacher who runs the Qur'an school
the one in front who leads the prayer
a scholar who issues rulings on law

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: he is tender-hearted, he will weep

s: Aisha pushed for her father to lead the prayer
she pushed back, saying he would weep too much to be heard.
when the Prophet ﷺ came out, he sent Abu Bakr back into the rows
he signaled stay where you are and sat beside him; Abu Bakr followed his prayer, and the people followed Abu Bakr.
Sunni and Shia Muslims read the scene's meaning for succession differently
many Sunnis see a sign for Abu Bakr; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet named 'Ali.

games.q: you're Abu Bakr, leading the prayer, and you hear the Prophet ﷺ come in, leaning on two men. what do you do?
o: keep going as if nothing happened.
stop the prayer to help him.
step back to give him the front.
games.why: Abu Bakr began to step back, and the Prophet signaled him to stay, then sat down beside him and prayed.

practice: Think of one place where you're usually in charge: the family group chat, the dishwasher, the meeting, the playlist in the car, the plan for dinner.
Picture handing it over for one day without correcting anyone, and notice what rises in you: relief, or itchiness. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to step back.

wordCard.voice: Imam. The one who leads the prayer, from a root meaning to be in front — the role the Prophet, too weak to stand, handed to his friend Abu Bakr. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who leads the prayer, from a root meaning to be in front.

carryVoice: Your line: let another lead. He handed it over, and stayed close by. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 664; 687; 713 (tell Abu Bakr to lead the people; Aisha's objection; he comes out and sits beside Abu Bakr)
